about: How much each topic matters for a production-grade LLM application. Modules are rated with a reason; lessons default to 2 unless listed.

scale.3: Essential: every production LLM app needs it
scale.2: Important: often needed, or depends on your use case
scale.1: Good to know: specialised, internals, or alternatives you rarely pick

langchain/01.why: Every LLM call goes through a chat model, messages, prompts and structured output.

langchain/02.why: LCEL chains are common for fixed pipelines; agents and graphs replace them for anything dynamic.

langchain/03.why: Tools are how a model reads your data and acts; schemas and error handling decide reliability.

langchain/04.why: create_agent is the standard agent loop: structured results, context limits and runtime context.

langchain/05.why: Retries, limits, guardrails and context control are what make an agent safe to ship.

rag/01.why: The whole pipeline end to end, and the scorecard every later change is judged by.

rag/02.why: Real company data is PDFs, Office files, HTML and email; whatever you can't load can't be answered.

rag/03.why: Needed when you have scans, photos or forms; skip it if all your documents have a text layer.

rag/04.why: Chunking is one of the biggest levers on retrieval quality, and it's cheap to tune.

rag/05.why: Picking the embedding model and store, and keeping the index in sync, is daily production work.

rag/06.why: Filters, hybrid search and reranking are where most production RAG quality gains come from.

rag/07.why: Grounded answers with citations and follow-up questions are what users actually see.

rag/08.why: Agentic, corrective, graph and multimodal RAG solve specific problems; add them only when measurements show the need.

rag/09.why: Evaluation, security, cost and latency: the difference between a demo and a product.

agents/01.why: State, nodes, edges and reducers are the base of every LangGraph app.

agents/02.why: Branches, loops and parallel work; the advanced parts (Send, Pregel) matter for complex graphs.

agents/03.why: Most production LLM systems are predictable workflows, not free-running agents.

agents/04.why: A tool-calling agent you fully control, with streaming to the UI.

agents/05.why: Conversations and long jobs must survive restarts; durable checkpoints are required in production.

agents/06.why: Required wherever an agent takes risky actions (payments, emails, deletes).

agents/07.why: Multi-agent systems add cost and failure modes; reach for them only when one agent clearly isn't enough.

agents/08.why: Config per user, async, retries, timeouts and tests: what keeps a graph running for real users.

agents/09.why: Deep agents suit long open-ended research or ops tasks; most apps don't need them.

agents/10.why: Memory, skills and harness control for deep agents: specialised.

mcp/01.why: Understand the protocol before relying on other teams' MCP servers.

mcp/02.why: Build servers when you expose tools to several AI apps; tools in depth matter most.

mcp/03.why: Using MCP tools from LangChain and LangGraph agents: common integration work.

mcp/04.why: Auth, authorization and security are mandatory once an MCP server is remote.

data/01.why: Text-to-SQL with safe execution: essential if your users ask questions about tables.

data/02.why: Agents vs workflows for SQL, approvals and accuracy evals.

data/03.why: Analytics extras: pandas, charts, semantic layer, files.

fastapi/01.why: Typed, validated, documented endpoints are how every LLM service is exposed.

fastapi/02.why: Streaming and background work are core to LLM APIs (long, slow responses).

fastapi/03.why: Authentication and tests are non-negotiable for a public API.

fastapi/04.why: Turning an agent into a service: SSE, concurrency, durable threads, background jobs.

production/01.why: Providers fail and cost money: timeouts, retries, fallbacks, budgets and rate limits.

production/02.why: Big savings for repeated questions, but semantic caches can serve wrong answers if tuned badly.

production/03.why: Without tracing you can't debug or explain a single bad answer.

production/04.why: Datasets, experiments and online evals are how you change prompts and models safely.

production/05.why: Containers, configuration, observability, CI and safe releases.

production/06.why: Kubernetes is common for larger deployments; many teams use simpler managed hosting.

production/07.why: Ingress, HTTPS, autoscaling and progressive delivery once you're on Kubernetes.
